title.en: Triam Udom Suksa M.4 English — Practice paper 2
title.th: ภาษาอังกฤษ สอบเข้า ม.4 เตรียมอุดมศึกษา — ชุดที่ 2

note.en: 60 questions in 75 minutes, weighted like the Triam Udom paper towards cloze, reading and error identification (tutor summaries report about 40 questions in recent years; ours is a longer practice paper). DeepDistrict practice — not an official or past paper.
note.th: 60 ข้อ 75 นาที เน้นเติมคำในบทความ การอ่าน และหาจุดผิด ตามแนวข้อสอบเตรียมอุดมฯ (ข้อมูลจากสถาบันกวดวิชาระบุราว 40 ข้อในปีหลัง ๆ ชุดนี้เป็นแบบฝึกที่ยาวกว่า) — แบบฝึกของ DeepDistrict ไม่ใช่ข้อสอบจริงหรือข้อสอบเก่า

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Agreeing to a request for help
skill.th: การตอบรับคำขอความช่วยเหลือ

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: Could you give me a hand with these boxes?
B: ______ Where do you want them?

explanation.en: 'Give me a hand' means 'help me', and B's next question shows B is helping: 'Sure, no problem.' 'Give me your hand' takes the idiom literally, 'I'm afraid I can' is not a natural reply, and 'Help yourself' invites someone to take food or things.
explanation.th: give me a hand แปลว่าช่วยหน่อย และคำถามต่อมาของ B แสดงว่ายินดีช่วย จึงตอบ 'Sure, no problem.' ส่วน 'give me your hand' แปลตามตัวอักษร 'I'm afraid I can' ไม่เป็นธรรมชาติ และ 'Help yourself' ใช้เชิญให้หยิบอาหารหรือของเอง

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การแสดงความเห็นใจเมื่อได้ยินข่าวร้าย

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: I can't believe I failed my driving test again.
B: ______ Third time lucky, as they say.

explanation.en: B adds 'Third time lucky', an encouraging saying, so B first shows sympathy: 'That's a shame — you'll get it next time.' 'Serves you right' means A deserved to fail; the other two are replies to good news.
explanation.th: B พูดต่อว่า 'Third time lucky' (ครั้งที่สามจะโชคดี) เป็นการให้กำลังใจ จึงต้องแสดงความเห็นใจก่อน ส่วน 'Serves you right' แปลว่าสมควรแล้ว และอีกสองตัวเลือกใช้ตอบข่าวดี

choices: That's a shame — you'll get it next time.

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การเสนอเป็นฝ่ายจ่าย

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: Shall we try that new Korean place for dinner?
B: I'd love to, but I'm a bit short of cash this week.
A: ______ It's my treat — you paid last time.

explanation.en: A says 'It's my treat', meaning A will pay, so A tells B not to worry about money. 'Let's go Dutch' means each person pays for themselves, which contradicts 'my treat'; 'Keep the change' is said to a waiter or driver.
explanation.th: A บอกว่า 'It's my treat' คือจะเลี้ยงเอง จึงบอกให้ B ไม่ต้องกังวลเรื่องเงิน ส่วน 'Let's go Dutch' แปลว่าต่างคนต่างจ่าย ซึ่งขัดกับการเลี้ยง และ 'Keep the change' พูดกับพนักงานหรือคนขับว่าไม่ต้องทอน

choices: That's fair enough, let's not go.

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การแสดงความคิดเห็นแบบมองสองด้าน

topic.th: บทสนทนาในชีวิตประจำวัน

items.stem:
A: Do you think the school should make uniforms optional?
B: ______ Some students would feel more comfortable, but others might be judged for what they wear.

explanation.en: B goes on to give one advantage and one disadvantage, so B is undecided: 'It's hard to say.' 'There's no downside' contradicts the disadvantage, 'I couldn't care less' shows no interest, and 'Not that I know of' answers a question about facts.
explanation.th: B ให้เหตุผลทั้งข้อดีและข้อเสีย แสดงว่ายังตัดสินไม่ได้ จึงตอบ 'It's hard to say.' ส่วน 'there's no downside' ขัดกับข้อเสียที่ B พูด 'I couldn't care less' แสดงว่าไม่สนใจเลย และ 'Not that I know of' ใช้ตอบคำถามเชิงข้อเท็จจริง

items.subject: eng

skill.th: กริยาวลี figure out

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วมและกริยาวลี

items.stem: Scientists are still trying to ______ how the virus spreads from animals to humans.

explanation.en: 'Figure out' means understand or discover. 'Turn out' means prove to be, 'run out' means have none left, and 'make out of' means build from a material.
explanation.th: figure out แปลว่าหาคำตอบ ทำความเข้าใจ ส่วน turn out แปลว่ากลายเป็น run out แปลว่าหมด และ make out of แปลว่าทำจากวัสดุ

items.subject: eng

skill.th: cause + กรรม + to-infinitive

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วมและกริยาวลี

items.stem: The heavy rain ______ the outdoor concert to be cancelled at the last minute.

explanation.en: Only 'cause' takes 'object + to-infinitive': 'caused the concert to be cancelled'. 'Made' and 'let' take a bare infinitive, and 'result' needs 'in'.
explanation.th: มีเพียง cause ที่ใช้รูป กรรม + to-infinitive ได้ ส่วน made และ let ตามด้วย infinitive ไม่มี to และ result ต้องใช้ result in

items.subject: eng

skill.th: อุปสรรคและปัจจัยเชิงปฏิเสธ

topic.th: การสร้างคำ

items.stem: The plan was rejected on the grounds that it was economically ______ and would need government money for ever.

explanation.en: After 'was economically' we need an adjective meaning 'cannot continue': 'unsustainable'. 'Sustainability' is a noun, 'unsustainably' an adverb, and 'unsustained' means 'not continued' rather than 'not able to continue'.
explanation.th: หลัง was economically ต้องใช้คำคุณศัพท์ที่แปลว่าไปต่อไม่ได้ คือ unsustainable ส่วน sustainability เป็นคำนาม unsustainably เป็นคำกริยาวิเศษณ์ และ unsustained แปลว่าไม่ได้ดำเนินต่อ ไม่ใช่ไม่สามารถดำเนินต่อได้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำคุณศัพท์ + บุพบท dependent on

topic.th: การสร้างคำ

items.stem: Thailand's tourism industry is heavily ______ on visitors from abroad.

explanation.en: 'Be dependent on' means rely on. 'Independent' means the opposite, 'dependable' means reliable, and 'is depended on' would reverse the meaning.
explanation.th: be dependent on แปลว่าพึ่งพา ส่วน independent มีความหมายตรงข้าม dependable แปลว่าไว้ใจได้ และ is depended on ทำให้ความหมายกลับกัน

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำปรากฏร่วม take responsibility

topic.th: คำปรากฏร่วมและกริยาวลี

items.stem: The minister refused to ______ responsibility for the failure of the project, blaming his advisers instead.

explanation.en: The collocation is 'take responsibility for'. 'Make', 'do' and 'have' are not used with 'responsibility' in this meaning.
explanation.th: คำปรากฏร่วมคือ take responsibility for (รับผิดชอบ) ไม่ใช้ make, do หรือ have

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ความหมายของคำคุณศัพท์จากบริบท

topic.th: คำศัพท์เชิงวิชาการ

items.stem: The professor's lecture was so ______ that half the audience had fallen asleep before the end.

explanation.en: Falling asleep shows the lecture was boring: 'tedious'. 'Riveting' means extremely interesting, 'concise' means short and clear, and 'provocative' means causing strong reactions.
explanation.th: การที่ผู้ฟังหลับแสดงว่าการบรรยายน่าเบื่อ คือ tedious ส่วน riveting แปลว่าน่าติดตามมาก concise แปลว่ากระชับ และ provocative แปลว่ายั่วยุให้เกิดปฏิกิริยา

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำกริยาเชิงวิชาการ undermine

topic.th: คำศัพท์เชิงวิชาการ

items.stem: Repeated delays and broken promises have seriously ______ public trust in the new transport system.

explanation.en: To 'undermine trust' is to weaken it gradually, which matches delays and broken promises. 'Underline' means emphasise, 'undertake' means begin a task, and 'underestimate' means think something is smaller than it is.
explanation.th: undermine trust แปลว่าบั่นทอนความเชื่อมั่น ซึ่งเข้ากับความล่าช้าและการผิดสัญญา ส่วน underline แปลว่าเน้น undertake แปลว่ารับทำงาน และ underestimate แปลว่าประเมินต่ำไป

items.subject: eng

skill.th: วลีตายตัว mutually exclusive

topic.th: คำศัพท์เชิงวิชาการ

items.stem: The two theories are not mutually ______; both may be partly true at the same time.

explanation.en: 'Mutually exclusive' describes two things that cannot both be true. 'Not mutually exclusive' matches 'both may be partly true'. 'Exclusively' is an adverb, and 'inclusive' and 'exhaustive' do not form this phrase.
explanation.th: mutually exclusive หมายถึงสองสิ่งที่เป็นจริงพร้อมกันไม่ได้ เมื่อเป็น not mutually exclusive จึงเข้ากับ 'ทั้งสองอาจถูกบางส่วน' ส่วน exclusively เป็นคำกริยาวิเศษณ์ inclusive และ exhaustive ไม่ใช้ในวลีนี้

items.subject: eng

skill.th: present perfect continuous

topic.th: กาล (Tense)

items.stem: I ______ for this bus for forty minutes, and it still hasn't come!

explanation.en: An action that started in the past and is still happening now, with 'for forty minutes', takes the present perfect continuous.
explanation.th: การกระทำที่เริ่มในอดีตและยังดำเนินอยู่ตอนนี้ พร้อมกับ for forty minutes ใช้ present perfect continuous คือ have been waiting

items.subject: eng

skill.th: เงื่อนไขแบบที่ 1

topic.th: ประโยคเงื่อนไขและ wish

items.stem: If it ______ tomorrow, the trip to the national park will be cancelled.

explanation.en: In the first conditional the if-clause uses the present simple even for the future: 'If it rains tomorrow, … will …'.
explanation.th: เงื่อนไขแบบที่ 1 ใช้ present simple ในอนุประโยค if แม้จะพูดถึงอนาคต: If it rains tomorrow, … will …

items.subject: eng

skill.th: It's high time + past simple

topic.th: ประโยคเงื่อนไขและ wish

items.stem: It's high time the government ______ something about the air pollution in the north.

explanation.en: 'It's high time + subject' is followed by the past simple to say something should already be happening: 'did'.
explanation.th: 'It's high time + ประธาน' ตามด้วย past simple เพื่อบอกว่าควรทำได้แล้ว จึงใช้ did

items.subject: eng

skill.th: relative pronoun whose

topic.th: อนุประโยคและคำเชื่อม

items.stem: The girl ______ bicycle was stolen reported it to the police.

explanation.en: We need a possessive relative pronoun (her bicycle → whose bicycle). 'Who's' means 'who is'.
explanation.th: ต้องใช้ relative pronoun แสดงความเป็นเจ้าของ (her bicycle → whose bicycle) ส่วน who's ย่อมาจาก who is

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Modal of deduction in the past
skill.th: modal แสดงการสรุปในอดีต

topic.th: รูปแบบกริยา (gerund/infinitive)

items.stem: You ______ have seen Mr Somchai at the market yesterday — he's been in Japan all week.

explanation.en: 'Can't have + past participle' means it is impossible that something happened. 'Mustn't have' is not used for deduction, and 'shouldn't' and 'needn't' give advice or lack of necessity.
explanation.th: can't have + V3 ใช้สรุปว่าเป็นไปไม่ได้ที่เหตุการณ์จะเกิดขึ้น ส่วน mustn't have ไม่ใช้ในการสรุป และ shouldn't, needn't ใช้บอกความไม่ควรหรือไม่จำเป็น

items.subject: eng

skill.th: โครงสร้าง the more … the more

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: The more you practise speaking, ______ you will become.

explanation.en: The structure is 'the + comparative …, the + comparative …'. After 'become' we need an adjective, so 'the more confident'.
explanation.th: โครงสร้างคือ the + comparative …, the + comparative … และหลัง become ต้องใช้คำคุณศัพท์ จึงเป็น the more confident

items.subject: eng

skill.th: regret + V-ing กับ to-infinitive

topic.th: รูปแบบกริยา (gerund/infinitive)

items.stem: She bitterly regretted ______ her best friend's secret to the rest of the class.

explanation.en: 'Regret + -ing' means feeling sorry about something you did in the past. 'Regret to tell' is used to announce bad news politely.
explanation.th: regret + V-ing หมายถึงเสียใจกับสิ่งที่ทำไปแล้ว ส่วน regret to tell ใช้แจ้งข่าวร้ายอย่างสุภาพ

items.subject: eng

skill.th: passive กับกริยารายงาน

topic.th: ประโยค passive

items.stem: The athlete ______ to have taken banned substances, but no proof has yet been found.

explanation.en: Other people make the claim about the athlete, so the passive reporting structure 'is alleged to have taken' is needed.
explanation.th: ผู้อื่นเป็นผู้กล่าวหานักกีฬา จึงใช้โครงสร้าง passive ของกริยารายงาน คือ is alleged to have taken

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การสลับที่หลัง Only after

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Only after the results were published ______ how serious the problem was.

explanation.en: A sentence beginning with 'Only after …' needs inversion in the main clause: auxiliary + subject + verb.
explanation.th: ประโยคที่ขึ้นต้นด้วย Only after … ต้องสลับที่ในประโยคหลัก: กริยาช่วย + ประธาน + กริยา คือ did the public understand

items.subject: eng

skill.th: เงื่อนไขแบบที่ 3 แบบสลับที่

topic.th: ประโยคเงื่อนไขและ wish

items.stem: Had the warning been issued earlier, many lives ______.

explanation.en: 'Had the warning been issued' is a third conditional without 'if', so the result needs 'might/would have + past participle'; lives are saved by others, so it is passive.
explanation.th: Had the warning been issued คือเงื่อนไขแบบที่ 3 ที่ละ if จึงต้องใช้ might/would have + V3 และชีวิตถูกช่วย จึงเป็น passive: might have been saved

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Subject–verb agreement with a compound subject
skill.th: ความสอดคล้องของกริยากับประธานสองตัว

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: My sister and I [[usually]] [[goes]] swimming [[on]] Saturday mornings [[before]] breakfast.

explanation.en: 'My sister and I' is a plural subject, so the verb is 'go', not 'goes'.
explanation.th: 'My sister and I' เป็นประธานพหูพจน์ กริยาจึงต้องเป็น go ไม่ใช่ goes

items.subject: eng

skill.th: การใช้ a/an ตามเสียง

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: He gave me [[an]] useful [[piece of]] advice [[about]] choosing [[a]] university.

explanation.en: 'Useful' begins with a /j/ (consonant) sound, so it takes 'a', not 'an'.
explanation.th: useful ขึ้นต้นด้วยเสียง /j/ ซึ่งเป็นเสียงพยัญชนะ จึงต้องใช้ a ไม่ใช่ an

items.subject: eng

skill.th: because กับ because of

topic.th: อนุประโยคและคำเชื่อม

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The documents [[were]] [[sent]] to the wrong address [[because of]] the secretary [[was]] new.

explanation.en: A full clause ('the secretary was new') follows, so we need the conjunction 'because', not the preposition 'because of'.
explanation.th: หลังช่องนี้เป็นประโยคสมบูรณ์ (the secretary was new) จึงต้องใช้คำสันธาน because ไม่ใช่บุพบท because of

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ความสอดคล้องในอนุประโยค that

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: There [[is]] [[a lot of]] evidence that [[regular]] exercise [[improve]] memory.

explanation.en: In the that-clause the subject 'regular exercise' is singular, so the verb must be 'improves'.
explanation.th: ในอนุประโยค that ประธานคือ regular exercise ซึ่งเป็นเอกพจน์ กริยาจึงต้องเป็น improves

items.subject: eng

skill.th: ผลของเงื่อนไขแบบที่ 3

topic.th: ประโยคเงื่อนไขและ wish

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[If]] I [[had known]] you were in hospital, I [[would visit]] you [[immediately]].

explanation.en: 'If I had known' refers to the past, so the result must be 'would have visited'.
explanation.th: If I had known พูดถึงอดีต ผลจึงต้องเป็น would have visited

items.subject: eng

skill.th: so กับ such

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The film was [[such]] boring that [[most of]] the audience [[fell]] asleep [[before]] the end.

explanation.en: Before an adjective alone we use 'so': 'so boring that'. 'Such' is used with a noun phrase ('such a boring film').
explanation.th: หน้าคำคุณศัพท์ที่ไม่มีคำนามตามใช้ so คือ so boring that ส่วน such ใช้กับนามวลี เช่น such a boring film

items.subject: eng

skill.th: No sooner … than

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: No sooner [[had we]] [[sat down]] [[when]] the phone [[started]] ringing.

explanation.en: 'No sooner' is always paired with 'than' ('No sooner had we sat down than …'). 'When' goes with 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely'.
explanation.th: No sooner ต้องใช้คู่กับ than เสมอ ส่วน when ใช้คู่กับ Hardly หรือ Scarcely

items.subject: eng

skill.th: much กับ many

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[Much]] people believe [[that]] the museum is [[the most]] popular attraction [[in]] the city.

explanation.en: 'People' is a plural countable noun, so it takes 'many', not 'much'.
explanation.th: people เป็นคำนามนับได้พหูพจน์ จึงต้องใช้ many ไม่ใช่ much

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำคุณศัพท์กับคำกริยาวิเศษณ์

topic.th: ความสอดคล้องและการเรียงคำ

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: The new manager [[speaks]] English very [[fluent]], [[although]] she has [[never]] lived abroad.

explanation.en: 'Speaks' is described by an adverb, so it should be 'very fluently'.
explanation.th: ขยายกริยา speaks ต้องใช้คำกริยาวิเศษณ์ จึงต้องเป็น very fluently

items.subject: eng

skill.th: insist on + V-ing

topic.th: รูปแบบกริยา (gerund/infinitive)

items.stem: Choose the underlined part that is incorrect: [[Despite]] [[being]] warned [[several times]], the tourists insisted [[to swim]] in the dangerous river.

explanation.en: 'Insist' is followed by 'on + -ing': 'insisted on swimming'.
explanation.th: insist ต้องตามด้วย on + V-ing จึงต้องเป็น insisted on swimming

items.subject: eng

skill.th: คำนามบอกปริมาณกับคำนามนับได้

topic.th: เติมคำในบทความ

items.passage: Every year the fashion industry produces more than 100 billion items of clothing, and a large (1) ______ of them are worn only a few times before being thrown away. This trend, often called 'fast fashion', has been made possible by cheap materials and by factories that can turn a new design into finished garments in (2) ______ of weeks. For shoppers the advantages are obvious: clothes have never been cheaper. The costs, however, are less visible. items.passage:
In the 1880s a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out an unusual experiment on himself. He memorised long lists of nonsense syllables — combinations such as 'WID' or 'ZOF' that had no meaning — and then tested how many he could recall after different periods of time. The results, plotted on a graph, produced what is now called the 'forgetting curve'. Memory dropped steeply in the first hour, and within a day he had lost more than half of what he had learned. After that the decline slowed, but it never entirely stopped.

Ebbinghaus chose nonsense syllables deliberately. Real words come with associations, and he wanted to measure memory without the help of meaning. This makes his findings something of a worst case: we forget meaningful material more slowly. Still, later researchers have repeated his experiment many times, and the basic shape of the curve has held up remarkably well.

The more useful part of his work concerned how forgetting could be slowed. Ebbinghaus found that each time he reviewed a list, the curve became flatter; he forgot less, and more slowly. Crucially, reviews were most effective when they were spaced out rather than crowded together. Studying a list ten times in one evening produced weaker long-term memory than studying it three or four times over several days. This principle, known as spaced repetition, is the basis of many modern flashcard apps, which calculate when a learner is about to forget an item and show it again at just that moment.

Why does spacing work? One explanation is that the effort of retrieving a half-forgotten memory strengthens it more than re-reading something that is still fresh. When information feels easy, the brain does little work; when recalling it requires a struggle, the memory is rebuilt more firmly. This also explains why testing yourself is more effective than simply re-reading notes, even though re-reading feels more productive at the time.

The implications for students are uncomfortable. The common habit of studying intensively the night before an exam can be enough to pass the next day, but most of the material will have disappeared within weeks. For subjects that build on earlier knowledge, such as mathematics or languages, that loss is costly. A schedule of short, repeated reviews takes no more time in total, but it requires planning — and the willingness to feel, for a while, that one is learning less.

items.passage:
In the 1880s a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out an unusual experiment on himself. He memorised long lists of nonsense syllables — combinations such as 'WID' or 'ZOF' that had no meaning — and then tested how many he could recall after different periods of time. The results, plotted on a graph, produced what is now called the 'forgetting curve'. Memory dropped steeply in the first hour, and within a day he had lost more than half of what he had learned. After that the decline slowed, but it never entirely stopped.

Ebbinghaus chose nonsense syllables deliberately. Real words come with associations, and he wanted to measure memory without the help of meaning. This makes his findings something of a worst case: we forget meaningful material more slowly. Still, later researchers have repeated his experiment many times, and the basic shape of the curve has held up remarkably well.

The more useful part of his work concerned how forgetting could be slowed. Ebbinghaus found that each time he reviewed a list, the curve became flatter; he forgot less, and more slowly. Crucially, reviews were most effective when they were spaced out rather than crowded together. Studying a list ten times in one evening produced weaker long-term memory than studying it three or four times over several days. This principle, known as spaced repetition, is the basis of many modern flashcard apps, which calculate when a learner is about to forget an item and show it again at just that moment.

Why does spacing work? One explanation is that the effort of retrieving a half-forgotten memory strengthens it more than re-reading something that is still fresh. When information feels easy, the brain does little work; when recalling it requires a struggle, the memory is rebuilt more firmly. This also explains why testing yourself is more effective than simply re-reading notes, even though re-reading feels more productive at the time.

The implications for students are uncomfortable. The common habit of studying intensively the night before an exam can be enough to pass the next day, but most of the material will have disappeared within weeks. For subjects that build on earlier knowledge, such as mathematics or languages, that loss is costly. A schedule of short, repeated reviews takes no more time in total, but it requires planning — and the willingness to feel, for a while, that one is learning less.

Subject: Proposal for a student-run repair café

Dear Dr Wanida,

I am writing on behalf of the Student Council to propose a new project for the second semester: a monthly 'repair café', to be held in the school canteen on the first Saturday of each month.

The idea is simple. Students, parents and local residents would bring broken items — bicycles, clothes, small electrical appliances, school bags — and volunteers would help them fix these items rather than throw them away. Similar events have been running in many countries for over a decade, and a secondary school in Chiang Mai started one last year with considerable success. According to its organisers, more than 300 items were repaired in the first six months.

We believe the project would benefit the school in three ways. First, it would give students practical skills that are not part of the normal curriculum, from sewing to basic electronics. Second, it would reduce the amount of waste our community sends to landfill, which supports the environmental goals in the school's development plan. Third, it would strengthen links between the school and the neighbourhood, since visitors would see students in a role of service rather than simply as customers.

We are aware that the project raises some practical concerns, and we have tried to address them in advance. Safety is the most important. Electrical repairs would only be carried out under the supervision of Mr Prasert from the Design and Technology department, who has kindly agreed to take part, and no item connected to mains power would be tested until he had checked it. We would also ask every visitor to sign a short form accepting that repairs are made on a voluntary basis and cannot be guaranteed.

As for costs, we expect them to be modest. Most tools can be borrowed from the Design and Technology workshop, and a local hardware shop has offered to donate basic supplies such as glue, thread and screws. The Student Council would use part of its existing budget to pay for refreshments.

We would be grateful for the opportunity to present the plan in more detail at the next staff meeting. If you approve, we hope to hold a trial event in November and review the results before committing to a full programme.

Yours sincerely,

Natthapong Srisuk
President, Student Council

items.passage:
Visitors to some of the world's most famous places are discovering a new item on their travel budgets: an entry fee for the city itself. Venice now charges day-trippers on its busiest days, and several islands and national parks have introduced or raised similar charges. Critics call these fees a tax on curiosity that will turn travel into a privilege of the rich. I disagree. Used carefully, they are one of the fairest tools we have.

Start with the problem they are meant to solve. When a small town receives more visitors in a day than it has residents, the costs are real, and they fall mostly on local people: crowded streets, rising rents as homes are converted into holiday rentals, and rubbish that the town's budget was never designed to collect. Tourists, meanwhile, often spend surprisingly little. A day visitor who arrives by coach, takes photographs and leaves before dinner may contribute almost nothing to the businesses whose streets they fill.

An entry fee shifts some of that cost back to the people who create it. This is hardly a radical idea. We already accept that visitors pay to enter museums and theme parks; the principle that a fragile place should be paid for by those who enjoy it is no different. If the money is spent visibly — on cleaning, on conservation, on housing for local workers — residents may even become more welcoming, since tourism stops feeling like something done to them.

The objection about fairness deserves a serious answer. A fee does make a trip slightly more expensive, but it is usually a tiny fraction of the cost of transport and accommodation. A family that can afford flights to Europe is not prevented from visiting by a charge of a few euros. Moreover, fees can be designed to protect access: lower prices for students, free entry for residents of the surrounding region, or charges only on the busiest days, so that those who are flexible can still visit for nothing.

None of this means that fees alone will solve over-tourism. A charge that is too low will change little, and one that is spent on unrelated projects will lose public trust. Fees work best as part of a wider plan that also limits cruise ships, controls short-term rentals and encourages visitors to explore less famous places. But to reject them as unfair is to ignore who is already paying the price of mass tourism: the people who live there.

items.passage:
Visitors to some of the world's most famous places are discovering a new item on their travel budgets: an entry fee for the city itself. Venice now charges day-trippers on its busiest days, and several islands and national parks have introduced or raised similar charges. Critics call these fees a tax on curiosity that will turn travel into a privilege of the rich. I disagree. Used carefully, they are one of the fairest tools we have.

Start with the problem they are meant to solve. When a small town receives more visitors in a day than it has residents, the costs are real, and they fall mostly on local people: crowded streets, rising rents as homes are converted into holiday rentals, and rubbish that the town's budget was never designed to collect. Tourists, meanwhile, often spend surprisingly little. A day visitor who arrives by coach, takes photographs and leaves before dinner may contribute almost nothing to the businesses whose streets they fill.

An entry fee shifts some of that cost back to the people who create it. This is hardly a radical idea. We already accept that visitors pay to enter museums and theme parks; the principle that a fragile place should be paid for by those who enjoy it is no different. If the money is spent visibly — on cleaning, on conservation, on housing for local workers — residents may even become more welcoming, since tourism stops feeling like something done to them.

The objection about fairness deserves a serious answer. A fee does make a trip slightly more expensive, but it is usually a tiny fraction of the cost of transport and accommodation. A family that can afford flights to Europe is not prevented from visiting by a charge of a few euros. Moreover, fees can be designed to protect access: lower prices for students, free entry for residents of the surrounding region, or charges only on the busiest days, so that those who are flexible can still visit for nothing.

None of this means that fees alone will solve over-tourism. A charge that is too low will change little, and one that is spent on unrelated projects will lose public trust. Fees work best as part of a wider plan that also limits cruise ships, controls short-term rentals and encourages visitors to explore less famous places. But to reject them as unfair is to ignore who is already paying the price of mass tourism: the people who live there.

explanation.en: 'Hardly a radical idea' is followed by familiar examples (museums, theme parks), showing the idea is not extreme or new.
